prompt: Candid documentary photo of a real serving of babi guling as eaten at a small Balinese warung in Ubud: the defining feature is blistered, puffed, bubbly, golden-brown CRACKLING — the spongy, crispy, puffy crackle armor that comes from spit-roasting a young pig over a coconut-husk fire for hours. The crackle must be visibly bubbled, with raised crispy bubbles, not smooth, not glazed, not shiny, not braised. A portion of tender pork meat attached to a piece of crackling on a chipped white plate: a slice of the spongy crackle, the meat layer beneath it still juicy. A small mound of steamed white rice. A small saucer of sambal matah (raw shallot + chili + lime + lemongrass relish). A small portion of lawar (chopped pork with grated coconut, long bean, and herbs). A wedge of lime. Served on a chipped plain white plate or banana leaf, on a worn wooden or formica warung table, a glass of iced tea (es teh) and a clay pot softly out of focus behind. Soft natural Balinese daylight from the open shopfront, viewed from about 40 degrees above, 35mm lens, moderate depth of field. Everyday unstyled serving, slightly messy edges, true-to-life colours, realistic textures. The crackle is the hero — visible bubbled, blistered, puffed golden-brown bubbles. Not glazed, not smooth, not braised, not curry-like, not soup-like. No food styling, no microgreens, no fusion garnishes, no studio lighting, no text, no logos, no people, no hands.
